fig.info.title: Eight movers, one scale
fig.info.what: Cost of transport, from the humpback whale (0.003) to a delivery drone (16). Log scale, lower is better.
fig.info.caption: An illustration, not a contest. Whale, eel, cyclist, walker and ASIMO are measured per kg of themselves; the Eco-marathon prototype, the ship and the drone per kg of passenger or cargo. Height follows the cost on a log scale; the horizontal order is by cost, not to scale.
chapter.sum.label: Summary
chapter.sum.title: There is no single most efficient mover
fig.lift.title: Lift a kilo by how much, for every metre you move it?
fig.lift.what: Cost of transport read as a lift: a COT of 0.1 costs the energy of raising 1 kg by 10 cm for each metre travelled. Height on a log scale.
legend.lift.payload: Per kg of passenger or cargo (payload)
fig.lift.caption: An illustration, not a contest: the two bases are never ranked against each other. Whale, eel, cyclist (rider), walker and ASIMO are measured per kg of themselves; the Eco-marathon prototype, the ship and the drone per kg of passenger or cargo. COT = energy / (weight x distance). Lower is better.
excerpt.text: There is a winner for each thing you choose to count
fig.champions.title: The champion of each class
fig.champions.caption: COT = energy / (weight x distance). Lower is better. Grades: A measured or official; B peer-reviewed model, synthesis or quoted review value; C manufacturer claim. The humpback whale value is derived from breathing, not from measured oxygen use.
chapter.s1.label: The Yardstick
chapter.s1.title: One number for a whale and a ship
fig.equation.title: One equation, no units
fig.equation.what: Cost of transport: the energy put in, divided by the weight moved and the distance
fig.equation.caption: Where a source gives energy and mass but not the cost of transport, the figure is computed from the inputs shown for each row. Oxygen is converted at 13.6 J per mg.
reading.yardstick.label: Yardstick
reading.bases.label: Two bases
reading.boundary.label: Energy boundary
reading.sources.label: Sources
fig.ladder.title: The scale runs across more than three orders of magnitude
fig.ladder.what: Every mover on one log axis, from the humpback whale (0.003) to the delivery drone (16)
fig.ladder.caption: Bars show the range where a source gives one; the dot is the central value. Filled dots are per kg of the mover itself, hollow dots per kg of passenger or cargo: the two are never ranked against each other. Passenger figures use a 75 kg person (EU type-approval driver mass); real passengers and Eco-marathon drivers can be lighter, which would raise the per-kg values.
chapter.s2.label: Living Beings
chapter.s2.title: Living beings: big swimmers win
fig.podium.title: The living podium
fig.podium.what: Cost of transport per kg of the animal itself, log scale. Lower is better.
fig.podium.caption: The humpback whale is the lowest number and the least direct: it is derived from breath counts and an assumed lung volume. Eel and beluga are measured oxygen use. The horse is a value quoted in a robotics review. Human rows are metabolic (food) energy: walking net of standing, walking fast (gross) and running.
fig.size.title: Size matters as much as medium
fig.size.what: Net cost of running against body mass, both on log scales: mouse to elephant
fig.size.caption: A model line from one published regression across 62 running birds and mammals (Taylor, Heglund & Maloiy 1982), not five measured animals. Net cost excludes the energy of standing still. Per kg, a mouse-sized runner spends about 47 times more than an elephant-sized one.
chapter.s3.label: The Human Body
chapter.s3.title: The human body and its best machine
fig.human.title: The bicycle more than halves the energy of walking
fig.human.what: Walk, run, cycle: cost of transport and food energy per km
fig.human.caption: Food energy, not electricity. Wh per km is food energy per person-km; for walking it is the incremental cost (range 56 to 88 Wh). ND: no defensible figure for that mode on the same basis. Muscles turn only about 22 to 25% of food energy into work.
chapter.s4.label: Robots
chapter.s4.title: Robots: still far from biology
fig.robots.title: Humanoids still spend ten times more than a walking human
fig.robots.what: Robots against two biological references, per kg of the machine, log scale
fig.robots.caption: All robot figures are total electrical energy, except BigDog (fuel). Cassie is a preliminary experiment. The Unitree G1 cannot be placed: Fraunhofer IPA publishes battery life but no distance or speed, so its cost of transport is ND.
chapter.s5.label: Moving People
chapter.s5.title: Moving people
fig.people.title: A record prototype uses 1.9 Wh per person-km; the UK road average, 213 times more
fig.people.what: Energy per person-km, sorted. Whiskers: car 1 to 4 occupants, double-decker 20 to 80 on board, and the spread across aircraft and Swedish city buses.
fig.people.caption: Each bar keeps its energy boundary: do not read the bicycle and the e-scooter as like for like. The Eco-marathon prototype is a one-seat car built only to minimise energy on a closed track at low speed: a physics limit, not a usable vehicle. The Candela ferry is a manufacturer claim (grade C); the double-decker bus and the eVTOL are scenarios or design models. COT per kg of passenger uses 75 kg.
chapter.s6.label: Moving Goods
chapter.s6.title: Moving goods
fig.goods.title: A ship moves a kilo about 1,176 times more cheaply than a drone
fig.goods.what: Energy per tonne-km of cargo, log scale
fig.goods.caption: Per tonne of cargo carried. Whiskers: the 10th to 90th percentile for ship and train. The long-haul electric truck is a scenario estimate, not fleet data.

footer.about: Astara Intelligence In Depth is a periodic analysis of the automotive and mobility sector for professionals navigating strategic uncertainty.
footer.disclaimer: Sources: peer-reviewed studies, national statistics, university and manufacturer releases (full list above). Cost of transport (COT) = energy put in / (mass x g x distance). Two bases are used and never ranked against each other: own mass (the animal, robot or whole vehicle) and payload (the passenger, counted as 75 kg, or the cargo). Living beings and human power are measured in food (metabolic) energy; machines in electricity or fuel delivered to the vehicle. Farming, power plants and refineries are not counted. ND means no defensible figure was found by the research cut-off; it never means zero, and nothing has been estimated. Prepared 3 November 2026; figures reflect published data as of that date and are subject to revision.
